strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exploiting known structure in combinatorial scientific-design objectives to improve sample-efficient optimization.

The proposed tree-factorized search distribution and use of descendant-aware local scores provide an intuitive, potentially useful connection among EDAs, graphical-model message passing, and policy optimization.
The manuscript is generally well organized and motivates the approach clearly, with helpful diagrams and extensive derivations.

The empirical study includes multiple sequence lengths, four principal protein-derived objectives, 20 optimization seeds, separate hyperparameter sweeps, and useful ablations over sampling budget and decomposition granularity.
weaknesses: The central derivation appears technically unsound. Equation 22 treats f(x) as equivalent to a sum of recursively defined Q-functions, but each Q-function already contains optimized descendant values; summing them double-counts subtree contributions. Sequential traceback can recover a maximizer under classical message passing, but this does not establish the claimed joint-objective or distributional equalities in Equations 23–24. Consequently, the lower-bound argument and the claim that the resulting factor updates optimize the original EDA objective are not justified.

Algorithm 1 is inconsistent with the mathematical definitions. Line 9 places a sum over all K samples inside the update for every sample, without normalization or conditioning on the current parent assignment. This is neither the conditional expectation defining V nor the single-trajectory Monte Carlo return suggested by the surrounding discussion, making the actual algorithm ambiguous and preventing faithful reproduction.

The experiments compare only against one naive autoregressive EDA. Essential controls are absent, including a tree-factorized EDA without descendant messages, policy-gradient/reward-to-go variants, classical exact message passing where feasible, FDA or related graphical EDAs, and relevant structured optimization baselines. Thus the gains cannot be attributed specifically to DADO's proposed message-passing mechanism.

The comparison is not demonstrably compute- or capacity-matched. DADO uses many separate MLPs and component evaluations, whereas the baseline uses one autoregressive model. Reporting equal numbers of sampled full sequences does not control parameter count, FLOPs, wall-clock time, memory, or objective-component calls.

The synthetic evidence uses only one randomly generated objective per sequence length; the 20 replicates vary optimization randomness rather than objective landscapes. The very small p-values therefore do not establish robustness across decompositions or functions.

The protein experiments optimize learned predictors rather than measured biological properties. Most underlying datasets are dominated by single/double mutants, while optimization may move far out of distribution; no experimental validation or reliable held-out evaluation of optimized sequences is provided. The paper explicitly sets oracle error aside, so these results do not substantiate the stronger practical scientific-design claims.

Predictor quality and the decomposition–accuracy tradeoff are insufficiently documented. Main experiments do not report held-out metrics for all protein predictors or compare against unrestricted predictors, making it unclear whether the optimized objectives are credible representations of the biological assays.

Hyperparameters are selected by the final optimization score on each objective, apparently without an independent validation protocol, and the reported tests reuse those tuned settings on the same landscapes. Multiple tests are also presented without correction. This can substantially overstate performance differences.

The novelty positioning is incomplete: the resulting local updates closely resemble standard policy-gradient credit assignment using reward-to-go on a tree. The claim that prior policy-optimization coordination is restricted to Markov chains needs much stronger support given broader work on factored policies, coordination graphs, graphical models, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and potentially useful idea: factorizing a search distribution according to a junction-tree decomposition and coordinating its factors using message-passing-style value functions.
DADO is motivated intuitively, connected to EDAs, policy optimization, and graphical models, and described in considerable algorithmic detail.
The experiments consistently show faster surrogate-objective optimization than the matched decomposition-unaware EDA, particularly as synthetic sequence length increases.
The appendix includes sample-budget and decomposition-threshold ablations, multiple protein datasets, implementation details, and results across 20 optimization seeds.
weaknesses: The central derivation contains a serious apparent error. Equation 5 (and equivalently Equation 22) asserts that maximizing the sum of the root and all subtree Q-functions is equivalent to maximizing f. These Q-functions contain overlapping descendant rewards, so the sum double-counts terms and can have a different maximizer even for a two-node tree. Consequently, Equations 6/23 and the subsequent lower-bound argument do not establish that DADO optimizes the stated objective. The algorithm may still be interpretable as a heuristic or policy-style update, but that would require a different, rigorous derivation or an explicit improvement theorem.

The protein experiments optimize and evaluate exactly the same learned decomposed predictor. There is no evaluation of generated sequences using held-out experimental measurements, an independent oracle, uncertainty-aware assessment, or even a second predictive model. These experiments therefore remain optimization of synthetic surrogates fitted to biological data and do not substantiate claims about practical protein design.

The empirical comparison is limited almost entirely to one naive EDA. Important alternatives are missing, including the Factorized Distribution Algorithm, standard evolutionary or coordinate methods, policy-optimization approaches, and exact/max-product optimization where tractable. Thus it is unclear whether gains arise specifically from the proposed message passing or merely from giving the optimizer the known factorization.

Each synthetic sequence length uses only one randomly generated objective; the 20 repetitions vary optimizer randomness rather than the landscape. The very small p-values consequently do not demonstrate robustness across problem instances, decompositions, or component-function families.

The claimed efficiency is evaluated only in sampling iterations. DADO uses many separately parameterized factors and sequential conditional operations, but the paper reports no wall-clock time, memory use, parameter-count comparison, or objective-evaluation cost. Statistical efficiency therefore does not establish computational efficiency.

Key experimental and reproducibility details remain problematic: protein predictor accuracy is largely omitted from the main evaluation, hyperparameters are selected directly by final optimization performance for every method-objective pair, and Algorithm 1 line 9 has a shadowed sample index and an apparently unnormalized sum where a conditional expectation or per-sample return is required. These issues make the reported comparison difficult to interpret and reproduce reliably.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exploiting known structure in combinatorial scientific-design objectives to improve distributional optimization.
The junction-tree formulation is intuitive, potentially useful across domains, and connects graphical-model message passing with EDAs and policy optimization in an interesting way.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful motivation, diagrams, pseudocode, and a substantial appendix.

Experiments consistently favor DADO over the matched decomposition-unaware EDA on synthetic objectives and several protein-derived surrogate objectives, with multiple sequence lengths, sample budgets, and random seeds.
The GB1 threshold study usefully illustrates the tradeoff between predictive accuracy, decomposition complexity, and optimization efficiency.
weaknesses: A central theoretical equivalence is incorrect. Equations 5/22 replace the sequential message-passing traceback with joint maximization of the sum of all Q-functions. This sum repeatedly counts descendant rewards and need not have the same optimizer as f. Even with one root and one child, the proposed expression becomes f_r(x_r)+2V_c(x_r) after optimizing the child, rather than f_r(x_r)+V_c(x_r), which can change the optimal root. Consequently, the transition to Equations 6/23 and the claimed distributional lower-bound objective do not establish that DADO optimizes the original objective.

Algorithm 1 does not correctly estimate the conditional value functions defined in the text. Line 9 sums a child's Q-values over all global samples, without conditioning on the current parent assignment and apparently without normalization. This yields a sample-independent scalar rather than an estimate of V_c(x_i); after mean-baseline subtraction, such a constant conveys no descendant information. The discrepancy makes both the claimed message passing and reproducibility of the implemented method unclear.

The weighted-MLE derivation defines an improved distribution proportional to f(x)p_theta(x), which is invalid when f or the Q-values can be negative. The experiments instead exponentiate shaped values. Although this ensures positive weights, applying a nonlinear shaping function independently to local Q-values is not covered by the derivation and may alter the coordination objective.

The empirical comparison is too narrow for a strong top-tier claim: the only primary baseline is one naive EDA. Comparisons to factorized EDAs, direct policy-gradient/return-to-go variants, classical max-sum message passing where tractable, local or evolutionary search, and relevant decomposition-aware Bayesian-optimization methods are absent.

The synthetic study uses only one randomly generated objective for each sequence length; the 20 repetitions vary optimization randomness on the same objective. Thus the very small p-values do not demonstrate robustness across problem instances, and hyperparameters are selected using final optimization performance on each tested objective.

The protein experiments optimize learned, deliberately decomposition-constrained predictors rather than experimentally measured fitness. They therefore demonstrate surrogate exploitation, not successful protein design. Main-text predictive accuracy, calibration, extrapolation behavior, and quality or plausibility of the resulting sequences are not adequately reported.

Important efficiency information is missing, including junction-tree clique sizes, parameter counts, runtime, memory use, and sensitivity to treewidth. DADO trains many factor networks and repeatedly evaluates component functions, so equal oracle-sample counts do not establish equal computational cost.

The reproducibility statement says that code is publicly available on GitHub, but the manuscript provides no repository URL. Together with the ambiguity in Algorithm 1, this prevents verification of what was actually implemented.

The idea and empirical trends are promising, but the central derivation and stated algorithm require substantial correction, and the evaluation does not yet isolate or convincingly validate the claimed message-passing mechanism. These are major rather than marginal issues.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: exploiting known structure to improve optimization over large discrete scientific-design spaces.
The proposed combination of factorized search distributions, local credit assignment, and message-passing intuition is potentially useful and is presented accessibly.
The empirical section includes several baselines, synthetic scaling studies, multiple protein datasets, 20 optimization seeds, topology perturbations, and runtime measurements.
The appendix provides substantial implementation and dataset detail and candidly reports settings where FDA matches or outperforms DADO.
weaknesses: The central derivation is technically incorrect. Equation 3 treats maximizing the sum of all recursively defined Q-functions as equivalent to maximizing f, but these Q-functions already contain descendant contributions, so the sum double-counts rewards. For a root r and child c, it optimizes f_r(r)+2 max_c g(r,c), rather than f_r(r)+max_c g(r,c); these can select different roots. Consequently, Equations 4–5 and the claimed lower-bound justification do not establish optimization of the stated objective.

Algorithm 1 does not correctly estimate the conditional value functions it defines. Line 9 sums every child's Q-value over all K samples for each outer sample, without conditioning on that sample's parent assignment and apparently without a 1/K normalization. This produces a shared constant rather than an estimate of V_c(x_i^k). If this is merely a notation error, the actual implemented algorithm still needs to be specified and reconciled with the theory.

The search-distribution factorization is underspecified and generally invalid for overlapping junction-tree cliques. A valid construction should generate only a child's residual variables conditioned on the separator, or explicitly enforce consistency for variables appearing in multiple cliques. The stated product over full overlapping meta-variables can sample duplicate, inconsistent copies.

The protein experiments are circular proxy evaluations: the authors impose a decomposition on a learned predictor and then evaluate generated sequences using that same predictor. There is no experimental assay, independent oracle, or reliable out-of-distribution validation of optimized sequences, so the results do not substantiate practical protein-design utility.

The empirical evidence is narrower than it first appears. Each synthetic dimension uses only one sampled landscape, with the 20 repetitions varying optimization randomness rather than landscape instances. The four emphasized protein tasks are selected from seven partly because they have favorable decompositions; in the appendix FDA outperforms DADO on two less-decomposable tasks.

Hyperparameters are selected using final-iteration performance on each objective, while significance tests are subsequently reported on that endpoint without accounting for selection or multiple comparisons. This weakens the inferential claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement says that code is publicly available but provides no URL, and several equations/pseudocode lines contain consequential notation errors. Given the mismatch among the stated objective, derivation, and algorithm, implementation access is especially important.

Because the primary theoretical justification is false and the experiments do not independently validate the optimized designs, the paper's central claims are unsupported despite the promising high-level idea.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: exploiting known structure in combinatorial scientific-design objectives to improve distributional optimization.
The junction-tree framing and combination of factorized search distributions with message-passing-inspired local updates are intuitively appealing and potentially useful.
The empirical section includes several baselines (EDA, FDA, and PPO), multiple sequence lengths and alphabet sizes, 20 optimization seeds, runtime measurements, and decomposition-robustness studies.
The appendix provides extensive implementation, dataset, and architectural details, and the protein datasets connect the method to scientifically relevant applications.
weaknesses: The central derivation contains a fundamental error. Equations 3 and 13 assert that maximizing f(x) is equivalent to maximizing the sum of all recursively defined Q-functions. These Q-functions already contain descendant contributions, so summing them double-counts subtrees and can change the optimizer. For a two-node tree, let root choice A have root reward 0 and best child reward 10, while B has root reward 8 and best child reward 3. The original objective selects B (11 versus 10), but the proposed summed-Q objective selects A (20 versus 14). Consequently, the claimed equivalence in Equations 4 and 14 and the subsequent lower-bound derivation do not establish optimization of the original expected objective.

The alternative maximum-entropy derivation also appears mathematically inconsistent: the stated value function V=log sum exp(Q) does not normalize exp((Q-V)/beta) for general beta. The correct temperature-dependent log-partition would require beta log sum exp(Q/beta). Thus this section does not repair the main derivation.

Algorithm 1 is not well-defined as written. Line 9 sums over all K samples while reusing the index k, lacks an apparent 1/K normalization, and seemingly assigns the same aggregate child contribution to every sample. This conflicts with both the stated Monte Carlo expectation and the per-sample update. It is unclear whether the implementation uses trajectory returns, conditional averaging, or the displayed formula.

Repeated claims of greater statistical efficiency are unsupported by theory. No convergence result, variance analysis, sample-complexity bound, or even direct gradient-estimator variance measurement is provided.

The protein experiments optimize and evaluate the same learned, deliberately decomposable predictor. There is no evaluation of proposed sequences using held-out experimental measurements, an independent oracle, or a stronger unconstrained predictor. The paper explicitly sets aside predictor error and out-of-distribution extrapolation, although these are central obstacles in protein design; therefore the experiments do not substantiate practical protein-design utility.

The synthetic evaluation uses only one sampled objective for each sequence length or alphabet setting. The 20 seeds vary optimization randomness rather than objective landscapes, so the very small p-values do not demonstrate robustness across functions. Moreover, singleton-node trees are an especially favorable special case and do not adequately test the claimed arbitrary-junction-tree setting.

The main text selectively emphasizes four of seven protein problems based partly on favorable decomposability. In the appendix, FDA outperforms DADO on GB1 and ynzC, while methods are nearly indistinguishable on CreiLOV. This materially narrows the empirical claim and shows that message passing is not consistently better than factorization alone.

The evaluation reports mean sampled predictor score and sometimes applies a visually amplifying negative-log transformation. Several results, especially AAV and Gcn4, have very large variance or appear influenced by late outliers. Median performance, best design under a fixed query budget, success probability, diversity, and untransformed effect sizes with uncertainty are needed.

Hyperparameters are selected using performance at the final optimization iteration on each evaluated objective, without a separate validation protocol. This creates optimistic method-specific selection and makes the reported comparisons less reliable.

The treatment of overlapping junction-tree clusters is insufficiently precise. Writing p(x)=p(x_r) product_i p(x_i|x_parent(i)) when clusters share variables requires explicit separator consistency and factors over only residual variables; otherwise variables are duplicated. The manuscript does not clearly formalize or verify this constraint.
The paper lacks a substantive discussion of biological safety, dual-use implications, or responsible release considerations despite presenting a method for optimizing protein sequences.

Because the claimed objective equivalence is false, the second derivation is also inconsistent, and the algorithm is ambiguous, the work has a serious central soundness problem rather than merely an incomplete evaluation. The empirical results may motivate a corrected policy-gradient-style method, but they do not validate the theory presented here.

strengths: DADO presents a clear and potentially useful idea: combining factorized search distributions with message-passing value functions to exploit known decomposition in discrete distributional optimization.
The paper is well motivated and provides substantial technical exposition, including connections to classical junction-tree optimization, EDAs, policy optimization, and a maximum-entropy alternative.
The synthetic experiments consistently show strong gains over EDA, FDA, and PPO as sequence length increases, supporting the claimed benefit in favorable decomposable settings.

The evaluation uses multiple protein datasets, 20 random seeds, method-specific hyperparameter sweeps, decomposition robustness studies, and runtime measurements. Comparisons with FDA help isolate the contribution of message passing from factorization alone.
The appendix is unusually extensive and the implementation, architectures, datasets, and hyperparameter ranges are described in useful detail.
weaknesses: The derivation does not establish that the practical DADO update monotonically improves the original distributional objective. It replaces a theta-dependent objective with a theta-dependent lower bound and then performs approximate factor-wise updates, but the consequences of optimizing this surrogate are not characterized.

Algorithm 1's Monte Carlo computation is technically unclear: estimating each conditional value V_c(x_i) generally requires child samples conditioned on each parent assignment, yet the algorithm appears to reuse one set of joint samples and even shadows the sample index k inside line 9. This ambiguity affects the central message-passing estimator and should be resolved mathematically and algorithmically.

The protein experiments optimize neural surrogate functions explicitly constructed to satisfy the assumed decomposition. They do not validate proposed sequences using assay measurements, an independent oracle, or even a non-decomposed predictive model, so they provide limited evidence of practical protein-design improvement.

Results are less consistent than the main-text presentation suggests. The four highlighted proteins were selected partly for favorable junction-tree structure; among the remaining three, DADO is statistically indistinguishable from the baselines on GB1 and is outperformed by FDA on ynzC and CreiLOV. This substantially narrows the demonstrated regime of advantage.

The central claim of statistical/sample efficiency is evaluated at only one sample count per setting. Curves versus sample budget, node size/treewidth, decomposition error, and value-estimator variance would be more diagnostic, particularly because performance deteriorates for larger junction-tree nodes.

Hyperparameters are selected using final-iteration optimization performance separately for every method and objective, involving up to 100 configurations. The selection protocol and seeds used for tuning are insufficiently specified, and the large tuning cost is excluded from the efficiency comparison.

The paper does not clearly explain how overlapping variables in adjacent junction-tree nodes are represented and sampled without duplication or inconsistency in the product p(x_r)∏p(x_i|x_parent). This is important because the protein junction trees explicitly contain overlapping positions.
